_about: The deliverables checklist's CATALOGUE: what a finished film has to hand over before anybody can play it. Content, so it lives here and not in deliverables.js — rule 2 in CLAUDE.md. The page renders every item and stores only the user's STATE against each `id` (fms_deliverables_v1), so an `id` is a storage key: edit a label freely, never an id.

`when` says who asks for it: 'always' (any screening at all), 'festival' (a festival or market), 'release' (a theatrical release or a streamer). The page filters on it. `formats` limits an item to 'feature' or 'short' projects; absent means both.

Indian specifics are stated carefully and should stay that way. The CBFC certificate is a legal requirement for public exhibition in India, not for a festival abroad; festivals in India screen uncertified films under an exemption from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting that the festival itself usually arranges. The ratings named are the ones in force after the 2024 Cinematograph (Certification) Rules: U, UA 7+, UA 13+, UA 16+, A, S. If that changes, change it here.

Festival-specific FORMATS are not listed here. They are derived at render time from the submission tracker (fms_festivals_v1) and festivals.json's `format` field, so a festival you add appears on the page with the format it asks for and nothing has to be kept in step by hand.
`tool` on an item names a tab of the same page that helps make it ('dialogue-list', 'certification'); the row links to it.

OPTIONAL GROUPS. A group with `optional: true` is a streamer's checklist and is OFF until the user switches it on for the film — its ids are storage keys like every other id, so they are new ids, never renamed ones. Each carries `source`, `sourceUrls` and `checked`. `published: false` marks a platform with no public delivery specification we could find: its items are a TEMPLATE for the spec sheet the platform sends you, and say so. Streamer specs change and are issued per title — the platform's own delivery requirements for YOUR title always win over this list.

groups.label: Picture masters
groups.blurb: The versions of the film itself. Make the top one first; everything else is exported from it.

items.label: Graded master — ProRes 4444 or 422 HQ
items.why: The one file every other deliverable is made from. Full resolution, final grade, final mix, with titles. Keep two copies on two drives.

items.label: Textless master
items.why: The same master with every title, caption and subtitle removed, so a dub or a territory version can lay its own text over clean picture. Asked for by every distributor and most streamers; nearly impossible to make after the fact.

items.label: DCP — Digital Cinema Package
items.why: What a cinema projector plays. 2K or 4K, SMPTE standard, unencrypted for festivals unless the festival asks for a KDM. Test it in a real cinema before you send it; a DCP that plays on a laptop can still fail on a server.

items.label: Screener — H.264, 1080p
items.why: What selectors watch. English subtitles burnt in, a private link rather than a file where you can, and a visible watermark if the film has not premiered.

items.label: Trailer or clip
items.why: Sixty to ninety seconds, from the graded master, with its own mix. Festivals ask for one for their programme and the press ask before anyone else does.

groups.label: Sound
groups.blurb: Delivered separately from the picture, because the picture gets re-cut for territories and the sound has to follow.

items.label: 5.1 printmaster
items.why: The theatrical mix. Delivered as six discrete channels, not folded into a stereo file.

items.label: Stereo fold-down
items.why: For the screener, the trailer, the web and any venue without surround. Made FROM the 5.1, never mixed separately, or the two will not match.

items.label: M&E — music and effects stems
items.why: The mix with the dialogue removed, so a dub can be laid in. Any sale outside the original language depends on it; the blueprint's post step already asks for it.

items.label: Music cue sheet
items.why: Every piece of music with its timecode, duration, composer, publisher and use (background, featured, title). Performing-rights bodies and streamers require it; without it the composer is not paid.

groups.label: Subtitles and access
groups.blurb: The film's words, outside the picture.

items.label: English subtitles — SRT and a timed master list
items.why: Timed to the graded master's frame rate. The single most common reason a Tamil film is passed over at an international festival is a subtitle file that drifts, is too long to read, or translates the lines but not the meaning. Have them read by someone who did not make the film.

items.label: Burnt-in subtitle version
items.why: A copy of the screener and, if the festival asks, of the DCP with the subtitles rendered into the picture.

items.label: Closed captions — SDH
items.why: Subtitles for the deaf and hard of hearing: dialogue plus sound description and speaker identification. Streamers and broadcasters require them; festivals increasingly ask.

items.label: Dialogue list — combined continuity and spotting list
items.why: Every spoken line with its timecode, in the original language and in English. The translator for every other territory works from this, not from the film.

groups.label: Certification and chain of title
groups.blurb: Nothing here is glamorous and every one of them can stop a screening.

items.label: CBFC certificate
items.why: Required by law for public exhibition in India — a theatrical release, a satellite sale, most Indian streamers. Festivals abroad do not ask for it. Festivals in India screen uncertified films under an exemption from the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, which the festival usually arranges. Ratings since 2024: U, UA 7+, UA 13+, UA 16+, A, S. Apply through the e-Cinepramaan portal with the final cut; a re-cut after certification needs a fresh certificate.

items.label: Chain of title
items.why: The paper trail proving you own what you are selling: writer's agreement, any underlying rights (a book, a true story, a remake), the director's and producer's agreements, and the company's incorporation. A distributor's lawyer will ask for all of it before money moves.

items.label: Releases — cast, crew, locations, music, artwork
items.why: Signed permission from every person on screen, every location, every piece of music and every artwork or brand visible in frame. Collected during the shoot, when the people are in front of you; near impossible to collect afterwards.

items.label: Errors and omissions insurance
items.why: Streamers and most distributors will not take delivery without it. It is issued against the chain of title and a title report, so those come first.

items.label: QC report
items.why: A technical check of the master against the buyer's specification: levels, dropouts, frame rate, loudness, subtitle timing. Streamers run their own and reject a file for a single fault, so have one run before you deliver.

groups.label: Publicity and festival materials
groups.blurb: What a selector, a programmer or a journalist opens before they press play.

items.label: Production stills — at least ten, high resolution
items.why: Festivals print them in programmes and the press use them whether or not you send any. Stills from the set, not frame grabs: a frame grab is 1080 lines and prints badly.

items.label: Poster — one-sheet, portrait
items.why: Print resolution, with and without credits block. The short-film blueprint's festival check already asks for it.

items.label: Logline and three synopses — one line, 100 words, 300 words
items.why: Every submission form asks for a different length. Write all three once, in English and in Tamil, and paste rather than rewrite under a deadline.

items.label: Director's statement, biography and photograph
items.why: A paragraph on why this film, a paragraph on who you are, a portrait that is not a selfie. The short-film blueprint's festival check asks for the bio; festivals ask for all three.

items.label: Full credit list
items.why: Every credit as it appears on screen, in a document. Programmes, databases and the CBFC form are all filled from it, and a misspelt name in a programme is forever.

items.label: Press kit — EPK
items.why: The stills, the synopses, the statement, the credits and the technical specification (running time, aspect ratio, sound format, language, subtitles) in one PDF. Running time to the second: it decides which festival sections you qualify for.

groups.label: Netflix
groups.blurb: From Netflix's published delivery specifications (Backlot help centre). What a given title owes is set by the Delivery Requirements List Netflix issues for it; this is the outline, not a substitute.
groups.source: Netflix Backlot help centre — Delivery Specifications (Version 5.1; enforcement of its changes began 2 January 2024), Dolby Vision HDR Mastering Guidelines, IMSC 1.1 Netflix Text Profile, Localization, Accessibility and Dubbing Branded Delivery Specifications. Read through search summaries: backlothelp.netflix.com was not reachable from the environment this was written in.

items.label: Delivery Requirements List for your title
items.why: Netflix issues one per title. It names which of the items below apply and adds anything else they want; when it and this list disagree, it wins.

items.label: IMF package — SMPTE ST 2067-21, Application #2E
items.why: Netflix takes its picture and sound as an Interoperable Master Format package to Application #2E (the 2016 or 2020 edition of ST 2067-21). Native frame rate, no pulldown flags; a package with immersive sound also follows the IAB Level 0 plug-in (ST 2067-201).

items.label: Dolby Vision HDR master — where the title is delivered in HDR
items.why: Netflix asks for HDR originals to be mastered in Dolby Vision and delivered as a Dolby Vision IMF package, from which it derives the HDR10 and SDR streams. A licensed SDR film may not need one: check the Delivery Requirements List before booking an HDR grade.

items.label: Audio — printmaster, stereo and the stems
items.why: The mixes and stems (printmaster, M&E, dialogue stems) your Delivery Requirements List names, inside the IMF. Make the M&E as you mix; recovering dialogue-free stems afterwards is expensive.

items.label: Non-subtitled version
items.why: Netflix's word for the picture without burned-in subtitles — titles and credits stay. If the film was finished with subtitles burned in for festivals, the clean version has to be conformed and graded again.

items.label: Timed text — TTML1, to Netflix's style guide
items.why: Subtitles and closed captions as TTML1 (.ttml/.xml) timed to the master's frame rate. IMSC 1.1 (Netflix's nst1 profile) is, per Netflix's own page, the format for JAPANESE timed text only; check before delivering IMSC for any other language. Follow the Timed Text Style Guide for the language. The dialogue list on this page is the subtitler's starting point.

groups.label: Amazon Prime Video
groups.blurb: From Prime Video's published Tech Docs (Video Central). Your licence agreement and Prime Video's per-title instructions decide the final list.
groups.source: Prime Video Tech Docs — Video requirements, Global packaging requirements, Audio, Captions and/or timed text, Dolby Vision & Dolby Atmos delivery requirements. Read through search summaries on 7 October 2026.

items.label: Video mezzanine — constant frame rate, correct flags
items.why: A constant frame rate, scan type and field order declared correctly in the file header, an accepted display aspect ratio, and no telecine (a telecined source is rejected; inverse-telecine it first).

items.label: Semi-textless master
items.why: Prime Video's term for a master with NO burned-in subtitles in any language, so that subtitles and dubs can be added as separate files. Package from component assets rather than one finished file.

items.label: HDR — HDR10 with a matching SDR, or Dolby Vision
items.why: An HDR delivery is HDR10, with a matching SDR source at the same resolution and identical runtime and conform. For Dolby Vision, a UHD SDR master and a ProRes 4444 (XQ) UHD HDR master with its Dolby Vision XML.

items.label: Audio — one asset per language, conformed to the picture
items.why: Each language as its own audio asset, conformed to the video mezzanine. The accepted channel layouts and loudness are on the Audio page; check them against your mix before you print master.

items.label: Timed text — DFXP/TTML, EBU-STL or iTT
items.why: Prime Video lists DFXP/TTML (.dfxp), EBU-STL (.stl), iTT (.itt) and, for Japanese only, Lambda Cap. SRT is NOT on that list: convert the subtitler's SRT before delivery. A forced-narrative track must match the main video's language.

groups.label: Aha — delivery template
groups.blurb: No public delivery specification from Aha could be found (checked 7 October 2026). These rows are the usual headings of a streamer's spec sheet, to fill in from the one their acquisitions team sends you — write what they ask for in each row's note.
groups.source: No published specification found; template only.

items.label: Their delivery specification, in writing
items.why: Ask for the spec sheet and the delivery schedule with the deal memo, before the grade is locked. Everything below is filled in from it, not from memory of another platform.

items.label: Picture master — in the format their spec names
items.why: Codec, resolution, frame rate, HDR or SDR, and whether they take a file, an IMF package or a drive. Note it here.

items.label: Audio — mixes and stems their spec names
items.why: Usually a 5.1 and a stereo mix, and often M&E or dialogue stems for dubbing. Note the layout and loudness target they ask for.

items.label: Subtitles and captions — formats and languages
items.why: Which languages, which file format, and whether captions for the deaf and hard of hearing are required. The dialogue list on this page is the subtitler's starting point.

items.label: Key art, stills and metadata
items.why: Poster and thumbnail sizes, synopsis lengths, cast and crew credits, and the CBFC certificate details most Indian platforms put on the title page.

items.label: Their QC pass
items.why: Most platforms run their own technical check and return a fault list. Note who fixes what, and by when.
